It is a matter of profound spiritual gravity to sit with the “unsearchable riches” of Christ while witnessing a world where “earthly kingdoms go the way of all flesh” through a “noise and tumult” of greed and neglect, and I must ask you with a gentle spirit: why do you ask after the relationship between extravagant wealth and the suffering of the saints in this hour? [3, 11, 13, 29, 692, 1503, 1605, Conversation History]. Are you perhaps feeling “overwhelmed and desperate” by the sight of “savage wolves” who “lie on beds of ivory” while the “horrible pit” of poverty swallows the faithful, or are you seeking a “settled certainty” to anchor your soul in the truth that the Master “sovereignly orders everything He has made”—including the final reckoning for the indifferent? [11, 13, 20, 1143, 1374, 1403, 1425, 1440, 1450, 1605, Conversation History]. In a day when many “shave off the edges” of the truth to offer “spiritual placebos” like the “prosperity gospel”—which suggests that “health and wealth are the birthright of every believer”—we must return to the “external Word” to see how the Lord personally governs the “vicissitudes of life” [1, 2, 11, 28, 313, 347, 1503, 1515, Conversation History].

The Reformed tradition teaches that “God personally and exhaustively pervades and sustains and governs every aspect of His creation,” and therefore, the disparity between the “glittery lookalike” of wealth and the “genuine commodity” of suffering for the name of Christ is not an “administrative anomaly” but a context in which the “spotless purity of truth” must be displayed [15, 68, 314, 1143, 1328, 1532, 1720, Conversation History].

### **Section 1: The Indictment of Indulgent Indifference (Amos)**

**Verse**
**“Woe to you who are at ease in Zion, and trust in Mount Samaria, notable persons in the chief nation, to whom the house of Israel comes! . . . Who lie on beds of ivory, stretch out on your couches, eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the stall; . . . Who drink wine from bowls, and anoint yourselves with the best ointments, but are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph” (Amos 6:1, 4, 6).** [646, 647, 779, 1019, 1321, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The sources teach that “wealth is not inherently evil,” yet it becomes a “sinful self-indulgence” when it leads to a heart that is “impervious to biblical truth” and “not grieved” by the “broken heart” of the suffering [60, 70, 196, 1238, 1406, 1422, Conversation History]. The Reformed faith—echoed by **John MacArthur**—asserts that “it is evil to love the gifts more than the Giver,” and those who “lie on beds of ivory” while neglecting the “affliction of Joseph” (the suffering of their brethren) prove that “sin is the monarch that rules the heart” (Romans 6:12) [70, 71, 581, 1262, 1365, Conversation History]. This indifference is a “wicked deed” because it ignores the truth that “your life is not your own” and that we are “stewards of whatever earthly resources the Lord entrusts to our care” (1 Corinthians 6:19; Luke 16:1–2) [12, 101, 113, 171, 174, 1138, 1262, 1406, 1670, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “not be deceived” by a “worldly philosophy” that measures your worth by a “balanced checkbook,” for “one’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses” (Luke 12:15) [12, 51, 91, 268, 1138, 1222, 1341, 1406, 1502, 1503, 1670, Conversation History]. Recognize that “he who trusts in his own heart is a fool,” and you must instead “discipline your mind” to “do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly” (Proverbs 28:26; Micah 6:8) [11, 116, 129, 251, 454, 697, 851, 1039, 1313, 1381, 1406, 1450, 1503, 1670, 1709, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Jewish vs. Gentile Context**
In the ancient **theocratic context**, “national greatness” and “beautiful cities” were often seen as “temporal signs” of God’s favor, yet the Jews were warned that “man shall not live by bread alone; but man lives by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3) [409, 1137, 1313, 1353, 1519, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our standing, showing that we are “sojourners and pilgrims” whose “citizenship is in heaven” and who find “repose of the soul” not in “storage cities” but in the “finished work” of Christ (Philippians 3:20; 1 Peter 2:11) [13, 21, 24, 26, 38, 142, 440, 1113, 1136, 1199, 1203, 1313, 1315, 1320, 1426, 1445, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 2: The Doom of Hoarded Riches (James)**

**Verse**
**“Come now, you rich, weep and howl for your miseries that are coming upon you! Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are moth-eaten. Your gold and silver are corroded, and their corrosion will be a witness against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have heaped up treasure in the last days” (James 5:1–3).** [1215, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed tradition—echoed by **Paul Washer**—teaches that “unbelief is the seed” of hoarding, for those who “trust in their wealth and boast in the multitude of their riches” forget that “the redemption of their souls is costly” (Psalm 49:6, 8) [1, 79, 1338, 1388, 1503, Conversation History]. James’s pronouncement of doom reveals that “endless personal accumulation is sinful and wasteful,” and the corrosion of the rich man’s gold acts as a “testimony” of his “unrighteous deception” (Luke 16:9; 2 Thessalonians 2:10) [189, 190, 1341, 1420, 1435, 1452, 1453, 1506, Conversation History]. Divine judgment falls on those who “lived on the earth in pleasure and luxury” while “practicing oppression and violence” against the poor (James 5:5; Jeremiah 22:17) [650, 967, 1215, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Trade in your worry for trust,” for the Lord is a “helper of the fatherless,” and He “demands a reckoning” for the mistreatment of the vulnerable (Psalm 10:14; Genesis 9:5) [6, 94, 201, 537, 589, 1270, 1294, 1408, 1515, Conversation History]. You must “not look for some other fountain of knowledge” in human “psychology or philosophy” to explain the judgment of the rich; instead, recognize that “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6) [11, 51, 123, 152, 209, 848, 1406, 1445, 1503, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Ritual to Reality**
Under the **Mosaic economy**, the “Year of Jubilee” was instituted to provide a “year of release from indebtedness” and protect the “poor and needy” from “rigor” (Leviticus 25:8–55) [397, 400, 1409, 1412, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our “redemption,” revealing that we have been “delivered from the slave market of sin” by the “precious blood of Christ,” and our “victory” is found in “our faith” rather than a temporal land lease (1 Peter 1:18–19; 1 John 5:4) [11, 24, 80, 136, 297, 1313, 1445, 1506, 1580, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 3: The Blessedness of the Afflicted (Christ)**

**Verse**
**“Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when they revile and persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely for My sake. Rejoice and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you” (Matthew 5:10–12).** [877, 915, 1231, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Scripture handles the “noise and tumult” of suffering by revealing that “blessedness” is the “repose of the soul who trusts in Christ’s finished work,” not a promise of “temporal happiness” [11, 13, 20, 24, 142, 1445, 1503, 1605, Conversation History]. To be “persecuted for righteousness’ sake” means identifying with a “Servant Savior” who was “smitten by God, and afflicted” (Isaiah 53:4) [11, 102, 359, 460, 485, 551, 738, 774, 832, Conversation History]. The Reformed tradition—upheld by **Voddie Baucham**—notes that “scars... don’t define us; our hope does,” for even as we are “afflicted in every way,” we find that “nothing thwarts any aspect of His plan” to give the kingdom to the “poor in spirit” (2 Corinthians 4:8; Job 42:2) [5, 11, 21, 246, 354, 569, 714, 851, 1132, 1408, 1441, 1515, 1572, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should find “tranquility of soul” by “resting upon the surest foundation,” for if you are “hated by all nations for My name’s sake,” you are merely “following in His steps” (Matthew 24:9; 1 Peter 2:21) [11, 24, 35, 45, 76, 116, 129, 201, 313, 325, 412, 655, 689, 743, 834, 1055, 1132, 1143, 1223, 1408, 1450, 1515, 1720, Conversation History]. “Wait for His Son from heaven,” knowing that “your labor is not in vain in the Lord” and He will “wipe away every tear from their eyes” (1 Corinthians 15:58; Revelation 21:4) [11, 14, 21, 24, 32, 94, 101, 109, 116, 121, 143, 201, 248, 286, 332, 352, 470, 718, 816, 822, 940, 948, 1132, 1143, 1153, 1313, 1315, 1406, 1408, 1426, 1450, 1515, 1709, 1720, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Continuity of the Decree**
Under the **Mosaic Law**, “false prophets” who “counseled rebellion” and nations that sacrificed their “sons and daughters” were subject to the “utter destruction” of the sword (Deuteronomy 13:5; 12:31) [95, 339, 345, 953, 956, 1316, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our “victory,” teaching that “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh,” but we still “contend earnestly” by “ascribing greatness to our God” through the “righteous deeds of the saints” (2 Corinthians 10:4; Jude 3; Revelation 19:8) [11, 21, 32, 43, 92, 125, 1081, 1210, 1313, 1515, 1646, 1670, Conversation History].

### **Section 4: The Fatal Weight of Indifference (The Rich Man and Lazarus)**

**Verse**
**“There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and fared sumptuously every day. But there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, full of sores, who was laid at his gate, desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man’s table. . . . The rich man also died and was buried. And being in torments in Hades, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom” (Luke 16:19–21, 22–23).** [208, 217, 218, 219, 653, 864, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The “record of history” reveals that the rich man was not charged with a “gross or notorious sin,” but was “selfish, uncaring, and stunningly oblivious” to the “destitute” neighbor at his gate [11, 15, 218, 221, 1143, 1532, 1720, Conversation History]. The Reformed tradition asserts that this is a “horrific and deeply unsettling story” intended to warn those who “cover their unbelief... with a veneer of hypocritical religiosity” [201, 214, Conversation History]. Divine judgment falls on indifference because “no slave can serve two masters,” and the rich man’s refusal to help Lazarus proved that “unrighteous mammon” was his true master (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13) [170, 196, 328, 1406, 1502, 1670, Conversation History]. This reveals that “God will not at all acquit the wicked,” for those who show “no mercy” will face a “merciless” judgment (Exodus 23:7; James 2:13) [26, 129, 138, 227, 762, 1056, 1201, 1317, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You must “discipline your body and bring it into subjection,” finding your “joy, satisfaction, [and] contentment” in “ascribing greatness to our God” by caring for the “least of these” (1 Corinthians 9:27; Deuteronomy 32:3; Matthew 25:40) [11, 13, 20, 36, 79, 101, 110, 116, 186, 1311, 1406, 1450, 1515, 1670, 1709, Conversation History]. Recognize that “every moving thing that lives shall be food for you,” but you must “not live by bread alone,” for your “inheritance incorruptible” depends on the “finished work” of the One who “made Himself of no reputation” (Genesis 9:3; Matthew 4:4; 1 Peter 1:4; Philippians 2:7) [13, 24, 26, 38, 136, 142, 440, 760, 830, 914, 974, 1214, 1251, 1313, 1426, 1445, 1503, 1506, 1529, 1580, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Continuity of the Decree**
Under the **Mosaic Law**, “the priests” were “messengers of the LORD” tasked with “ensure[ing] justice for all,” yet they often “rule[d] by their own power” and “neglected the weightier matters” (Malachi 2:7; Jeremiah 5:31; Matthew 23:23) [8, 14, 130, 341, 751, 847, 848, 1091, 1092, 1316, 1317, 1365, 1422, 1473, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** the structure of the household of faith, revealing that “Jesus Christ alone is the head of the church,” and any “religious court” or “politician” who offers “protection” in exchange for jurisdiction over “teaching and mercy” is a “spirit of fraud” [11, 19, 68, 95, 122, 186, 239, 279, 284, 285, 286, 289, 293, 317, 343, 345, 348, 359, 361, 402, 403, 412, 415, 558, 598, 1130, 1144, 1233, 1314, 1316, 1411, 1418, 1431, 1503, 1528, 1627, 1636, 1638, 1720, Conversation History].

**Final Reminder**
**“Nevertheless the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, ‘The Lord knows those who are His,’ and, ‘Everyone who names the name of the Lord is to abstain from wickedness’ ” (2 Timothy 2:19).** [11, 87, 147, 176, 201, 211, 222, 282, 285, 300, 311, 324, 332, 335, 361, 405, 413, 414, 444, 449, 591, 1138, 1407, 1441, 1450, Conversation History].

references.cited_text: In one of his dreams, Daniel saw a statue representing the kingdoms of the world smashed to pieces by a flying stone, which represents Christ (Dan. 2:34–35). Then the stone filled the whole earth. The symbolism is clear: Christ ultimately crushes the kingdoms of men and establishes His own. Christ is inseparable from His kingdom. The holy purpose of God is to exalt Christ in the consummation of history when the Son rules and reigns in His kingdom. The Jewish Talmud is right in saying that the prayer in which there is no mention of the kingdom of God is not a prayer at all (Berakoth 21a).

A single pearl of perfection, size, and beauty could be of immense value. When Jesus said, “Do not … cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6), He was painting an absurd word picture to illustrate the folly of attempting to reason with people who clearly have nothing but contempt for the truth. Who would ever expect the lowest of unclean brute beasts to appreciate something as valuable as pearls? This merchant sought fine pearls to sell because they were a reliable investment; they increased in value as time went by. As is true today, wise investors would diversify: put some money in the ground, some in pearls, some in real estate. The one thing smart investors did not typically do was put everything into one commodity.

There’s no question, however, that the point of this parable was especially significant for the Pharisees. It was a direct blow to the very heart of their belief system. They were not only self-righteous; they were obnoxiously so. They constantly viewed others with contempt (Luke 7:39; 15:2; John 7:47–49; 9:34). And we know that Pharisees were constantly present whenever Jesus taught publicly because they were desperately looking for reasons to accuse Him. Just two chapters earlier, in Luke 16:14, we read, “The Pharisees … heard all these things, and they derided Him.” Jesus’ reply to them in that text strikes the same note as our parable: “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is highly esteemed among men is an abomination in the sight of God” (v. 15).

The Story The main character in this parable is a man whom Jesus refers to as an “unjust steward” (Luke 16:8). So there’s no question about his crooked character. The steward’s own actions reveal that he was wicked, conniving, totally unprincipled, and shamelessly brazen in his evildoing. But he apparently got to that point by a progression of compromises that probably seemed petty at first. His downfall began because he handled his master’s assets in a way that was wasteful—overspending, or perhaps using company resources to pay for personal expenses. He must have figured he was free to spend extravagantly because the master would never check up on him. But a credible accusation against him reached the ears of his wealthy boss, who subsequently gave him his termination notice and ordered a full audit.

He indicated, for example, that hell will be full of religious people. According to Scripture, multitudes of seemingly devout and philanthropic people (including some self-styled miracle workers) will be astonished when they are turned away at the throne of judgment. Jesus made that point emphatically: “Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of My Father in heaven. Many will say to Me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in Your name, cast out demons in Your name, and done many wonders in Your name?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness!’ ” (Matt. 7:21–23, emphasis added). Those turned away will include not only people who are ensnared in cults and false religions, but also confessionally orthodox people who don’t truly believe what they profess. Such people cover their unbelief and secret sins with a veneer of hypocritical religiosity.

Knowing the Terror of the Lord Obviously, Jesus was not telling this story for anyone’s amusement. This is a solemn, earnest word of warning— precisely the kind of testimony the rich man in the parable was begging to be delivered to his five brothers. If the story slams you with a feeling of shock or dismay, that was precisely Jesus’ intent. The severity of the subject matter is exceeded only by the urgency of the point our Lord was making. This is hard-edged teaching—on purpose. Jesus is not concerned here

Notice also that when the rich man finds himself in hell, he does not ask for reconsideration or release on the grounds of pity or mercy. He doesn’t say, “Someone made a mistake!” He doesn’t ask, “Why am I here?” All pretense has now been stripped away and he is under the full weight of his own guilt. He knows he deserves to be in hell. All he asks for is the smallest hint of relief. He’s never going to get that. There is no hope of a moment’s pause in the grinding, eternal, bitter accusations of his own guilty conscience. The only concern he has left is for his brothers, because he knows they are exactly like him— respectable, complacent, comfortably wealthy pillars of society, doing whatever they want, going through the motions of enough religious activity to maintain an honorable reputation, but headed directly for hell.

As Paul explained to Timothy: The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, “The Lord knows those who are His,” and, “Everyone who names the name of the Lord is to abstain from wickedness.” Now in a large house there are not only gold and silver vessels, but also vessels of wood and of earthenware, and some to honor and some to dishonor. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to the Master, prepared for every good work. Now flee from youthful lusts and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart. (2 Tim. 2:19–22)
